note: ß upper-cases to SS in both Python str.upper() and JS toUpperCase(); casefold()/toLocaleLowerCase() disagree on this, which was the original LW09 bug.
U+0130 (dotted capital I) upper/lowers to 'i' + combining dot above (U+0307) under non-locale casing in both languages, not plain 'i'.
U+0131 (dotless small i) upper-cases to plain 'I' in both languages under non-locale casing.
U+FB01 (ﬁ ligature) has a compatibility decomposition to 'fi' applied by NFKC in both languages.
Fullwidth Latin letters (U+FF21...) decompose to ASCII under NFKC in both languages.
'e' + combining acute (U+0301) composes to precomposed 'é' (U+00E9) under NFKC in both languages.
Leading/trailing NBSP (U+00A0) and ASCII space are both in the shared explicit trim character set.
Python str.lower()/upper() and JS toLowerCase()/toUpperCase() apply the same context-sensitive Greek sigma casing, so both round-trip to the same form.
U+200B (zero-width space) is category Cf, not Zs, and is deliberately excluded from the shared trim character set in both languages, so it is not silently discarded.

U+FEFF (BOM/ZWNBSP) is deliberately excluded from the shared trim character set in both languages; JS's built-in trim() removes it but Python's strip() does not, which is exactly the asymmetry this fixture guards against. Using the shared explicit charset on both sides keeps this a consistent non-match instead of a silent divergence.

U+0085 (NEL) is deliberately excluded from the shared trim character set in both languages; Python's built-in strip() removes it but JS's trim() does not. Using the shared explicit charset on both sides keeps this a consistent non-match instead of a silent divergence.
ASCII tab is in the shared explicit trim character set in both languages, so leading/trailing tabs are discarded identically.
